African elephant neonates are notably precocial, with newborn calves able to stand within hours of parturition. At birth, the calf typically measures around 90 cm [Lb = around 90 cm] at the shoulder, a stature that allows it to keep pace with the maternal herd almost immediately. The corresponding wet weight at birth averages approximately 105,000 grams [Wwb = approximately 105,000 grams], reflecting the substantial investment characteristic of this long-lived species. This large neonatal size is an adaptation to the challenging savanna environment, where predation pressure on the young is significant despite the protective vigilance of the herd. The growth trajectory from this substantial birth mass toward the adult form is remarkably rapid during the first few years of life, supported by intensive maternal care and a prolonged period of nutritional dependency. Field records indicate that the time since birth at weaning is approximately 1,071 days [tx = approximately 1,071 days] at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], a lengthy nursing period that underscores the importance of milk as a transitional food source while the juvenile develops the dentition and digestive efficiency required to process coarse vegetation.

Reproductive timing in the African elephant is characterised by an exceptionally long gestation, even by the standards of other large terrestrial mammals. Extensive field studies in East Africa have documented that the gestation period lasts approximately 670 days [tg = approximately 670 days], a duration that accommodates the extensive foetal development and organogenesis required to produce a precocial calf of over at a temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C] 100,000 grams. This prolonged gestation interval is tied to the species' stable, warm-body temperature of around 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], under which all key life-history processes operate. Following birth, the suckling juvenile enters a phase of rapid skeletal elongation that continues through the pre-weaning period. Shoulder height at weaning, recorded at about 135 cm , represents a nearly fifty percent increase from the neonatal value, highlighting the intense growth phase supported by maternal milk, with body mass at this stage reaching approximately 600,000 grams [Wwx = approximately 600,000 grams]. This solid food transition marks a critical juncture in the life cycle, after which the weaned juvenile must rely entirely on its own foraging abilities.

The transition to adolescence is marked by significant morphological and physiological changes, including the attainment of reproductive capacity. In free-ranging populations inhabiting typical savanna ecosystems with a mean body temperature maintained at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 4,018 days [tp = approximately 4,018 days], which corresponds to roughly eleven years of age. At this point, shoulder height at puberty averages roughly 230 cm [Lp = roughly 230 cm], a dimension that signals the near-completion of the skeletal growth trajectory. This relatively late onset of sexual maturation is consistent with the species' slow life-history pace, a pattern driven by the substantial energy demands of attaining such a large body size before reproductive effort can be initiated. The pubertal individual, though capable of gametogenesis, often delays actual breeding for several additional years due to social suppression by dominant adults and the need to accumulate sufficient body condition. This reproductive quiescence allows for continued somatic expansion and the learning of complex social behaviours crucial for future reproductive success under the stable thermal conditions of their environment.

The ultimate dimensions of the African elephant reflect its status as the largest extant terrestrial animal, with adults exhibiting pronounced sexual dimorphism. The maximum shoulder height achieved by mature individuals reaches approximately 250 cm [Li = approximately 250 cm], a stature that grants unparalleled access to high-canopy browse and confers a formidable defense against most predators. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for a fully grown adult can reach as high as 4,800,000 grams [Wwi = 4,800,000 grams], representing a more than forty-five-fold increase from the neonatal mass. Achieving this enormous adult body mass requires decades of sustained foraging, and the daily plant intake at ultimate size has been measured at roughly 450,000 grams per day  under the species' typical core body temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This massive food intake drives the well-known ecological role of elephants as ecosystem engineers, as their feeding activities modify vegetation structure across vast landscapes. The energy budget required to sustain such a large body is a major constraint on population density, particularly during dry-season resource bottlenecks.

The lifespan of the African elephant ranks among the longest of any terrestrial mammal, with individuals routinely surviving for many decades in both protected and wild settings. Maximum recorded longevity for this species reaches approximately 29,200 days [am = approximately 29,200 days] at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], which equates to about eighty years, a duration that allows for multiple reproductive events across a female's lifetime. This extended lifespan is intricately linked to the species' very low maximum reproductive rate, which under the stable temperature regime of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C] averages approximately one calf per birth event [N_R_i = approximately one calf per birth event] with an inter-birth interval of roughly 5 years [F_R_i = an inter-birth interval of roughly 5 years]. The combination of a single calf per birth event and inter-birth intervals spanning several years means that a female can produce, at most, a handful of offspring over her long life. This slow life-history strategy, characterised by high maternal investment in each calf and a protracted developmental schedule, is typical of K-selected megafauna facing low extrinsic mortality. The social structure of matriarchal herds provides critical knowledge transfer across generations, enabling naïve individuals to navigate resource fluctuations and predation threats during the extended juvenile and sub-adult phases that precede their own reproductive activity.
